prompt:
You are a world-class expert: an economist by training who later spent two decades as a senior strategy advisor to executives at large enterprise software companies.

I lead engineering for a mid-sized company whose core product is a 20-year-old policy administration system for property and casualty insurers. It still works and it runs most of our revenue, but every new feature takes months, our best engineers keep leaving, and two competitors now market themselves as "cloud-native." Our CTO believes we must rewrite the platform from scratch on a modern stack over the next two years, because incremental fixes will never get us out of the hole. Our head of product believes we should modernize incrementally, carving off one capability at a time behind the existing system while continuing to ship features customers are asking for. Which strategy is right?
response:
**Short answer:** Your head of product is closer to right, but not for the reasons usually given, and only if the incremental plan takes your CTO's diagnosis seriously. A from-scratch rewrite of a P&C policy admin system is one of the highest-risk bets in enterprise software. "Incremental modernization" is also how many companies spend five years going nowhere. The real choice is between a disciplined, funded, architecturally directed migration and everything else.

## Why the rewrite is worse than it looks

**1. In your market, a rewrite is a customer migration program, not an engineering project.** Your customers have configured their products, rating algorithms, forms, and workflows on your current system. Many of those rates and rules are filed with state regulators and must be reproduced exactly. They carry in-force policies that will renew, endorse, cancel, and reinstate, sometimes out of sequence, for years. Even if you ship a new platform in two years, each carrier must run its own re-implementation and data conversion, which is typically a 12–24 month project it has to budget for, staff, and justify to its board. Some will refuse. Realistically, you will run two platforms for five to eight years. The rewrite doesn't replace your legacy burden. It doubles it for most of a decade.

**2. The payoff is binary and back-loaded; the costs are front-loaded and certain.** A rewrite delivers roughly zero customer value until it reaches feature parity, and parity with a 20-year-old system is a moving, poorly specified target. That old code encodes two decades of edge cases, regulatory fixes, and customer-specific behavior that nobody fully documented. Schedule risk on projects like this is fat-tailed: they rarely run 20% over, and they often run 100–200% over. Meanwhile:
- Feature work on the current product slows or stops, while competitors keep shipping and your customers keep evaluating them at renewal.
- You face an Osborne effect. Announcing a new platform tells customers the current one is a dead end, which chills upsell and invites RFPs.
- You create a two-caste engineering org: the exciting new-platform team and the people keeping the lights on. The second group holds the domain knowledge the first desperately needs, and they will be the next to leave.

**3. It destroys option value.** Incremental work lets you learn and redirect every quarter. A rewrite commits you to a two-year-old set of assumptions about architecture, market, and priorities.

## Where your CTO is right

Don't dismiss the CTO's argument. Incremental modernization genuinely fails in predictable ways:
- **No target architecture.** Teams refactor whatever is annoying this sprint, and nothing structurally changes.
- **No protected funding.** Every quarter, customer features win the capacity argument, and modernization gets the leftovers.
- **Nothing gets retired.** New services get built alongside old code that never gets switched off, so complexity goes up.
- **Nibbling at the edges forever.** Teams extract easy peripheral pieces and never touch the core that actually slows you down.

If your head of product's version of "incremental" means "keep shipping features and modernize when we can," the CTO is correct that it will never get you out of the hole.

## What I'd recommend: incremental with teeth

**Adopt the CTO's diagnosis as the constraints on the head of product's strategy.**

1. **Define an explicit target architecture**, the end state you're migrating toward. It should be concrete enough that every extraction can be judged against it.
2. **Ring-fence capacity.** Commit a fixed share of engineering to modernization, typically 30–40%, protected at the executive level and not renegotiated each quarter.
3. **Put an API and anti-corruption layer in front of the legacy system.** New capabilities call the facade, never the old internals. Use change-data-capture from the legacy database so new services can consume events without deep coupling.
4. **Sequence extractions by change frequency multiplied by separability.** Start where you feel the most pain and the seams are cleanest. In policy admin, that usually means:
   - rating and rules
   - document and forms generation
   - integrations and APIs
   - reporting and data
   - sometimes billing

   Leave the core policy transaction model (the heart of issuance, endorsement, and renewal) until later, after you've built skill and confidence.
5. **Measure retirement, not construction.** Track the share of transactions flowing through new components and the lines or modules actually decommissioned. If legacy scope isn't shrinking, the program is failing, whatever the demos look like.
6. **Tie modernization to features customers are asking for.** When customers demand better rating flexibility, that's your reason to extract rating. The feature funds the modernization and proves it.

## Separate the three problems you're actually facing

The rewrite debate bundles three distinct problems, and each has a cheaper, faster fix than a rewrite:

- **"Competitors are cloud-native."** Find out what buyers actually mean. Carriers usually want vendor-operated SaaS, painless upgrades, modern APIs, and faster product configuration. Architectural purity is rarely the point. You can offer a managed cloud-hosted version of the current system and a clean API layer within a year. That neutralizes most of the marketing gap while real modernization proceeds.
- **"Features take months."** Diagnose why before prescribing. Is it code coupling, a missing test suite, manual deployment, or a painful configuration model? Automated regression testing around rating and transaction behavior is often the single highest-return investment. It also happens to be a prerequisite for any safe migration.
- **"Our best engineers are leaving."** Engineers leave over tedium, fear of breaking things, and career dead ends more than over language choice. A credible modernization program where people get to build new services, rotate between legacy and new work, and see progress retains people. So does paying legacy experts as the critical asset they are.

## When a rewrite *would* be right

Be fair to the CTO. A clean-sheet build makes sense if:
- the technology stack is approaching true end-of-life, with an unsupported runtime or unpatchable security exposure;
- the system has genuinely no extractable seams, which is rarer than people claim; or
- you're targeting a new segment, such as small commercial, specialty, or MGAs, where there's no migration burden.

That last case is the interesting one. A greenfield product for a new market, built on the same extracted services as your modernization, gives the CTO a clean build without betting the installed base on it.

## How to settle it

Ask each leader to put numbers on paper: expected customer migration timeline, revenue at risk during transition, parity scope, and staffing. Then ask them to say what evidence at the 6- and 12-month marks would prove their approach is failing. The rewrite plan will struggle to answer the migration question honestly. The incremental plan will struggle to show how it reaches the core. Whichever plan survives that exercise is your strategy. In my experience, for a revenue-carrying P&C system, it's almost always the disciplined incremental one.
summary:
The response concludes that the head of product is closer to right, but only if incremental modernization is disciplined enough to answer the CTO's concerns. It frames the real choice as a funded, architecturally directed migration versus everything else.

It argues a rewrite is worse than it looks. For P&C carriers, a rewrite becomes a customer migration program. Regulator-filed rates and rules must be reproduced exactly, in-force policies must keep working, and each carrier faces its own 12–24 month conversion. The likely result is running two platforms for five to eight years. The costs are certain and front-loaded, while the payoff is binary and delayed until parity with poorly documented legacy behavior. Schedules often run 100–200% over. Feature work stalls, an Osborne effect chills sales, a two-caste engineering org drives out domain experts, and option value disappears.

The CTO is right that incremental efforts often fail. They lack a target architecture and protected funding, never retire old code, and only nibble at the edges.

Its recommendation is "incremental with teeth":
- Define a concrete target architecture.
- Ring-fence 30–40% of capacity for modernization.
- Put an API and anti-corruption layer, plus change-data-capture, in front of the legacy system.
- Sequence extractions by change frequency times separability, starting with rating and rules, documents, integrations, reporting, and possibly billing, and leaving the core policy transaction model for later.
- Measure retirement rather than construction.
- Tie extractions to features customers are requesting.

It separates three underlying problems. It suggests offering managed cloud hosting and APIs within a year, diagnosing why features are slow (with automated regression testing as a top investment), and retaining engineers through meaningful work, rotation, and pay.

A rewrite fits only when the stack is at true end-of-life, the system has no extractable seams, or the company is building a greenfield product for a new segment. To settle the debate, it suggests having each leader quantify migration timelines, revenue at risk, parity scope, and staffing, and name the 6- and 12-month evidence that would show their plan is failing.
